name_en: Li Zhi Hong Cha (Lychee Black Tea)
processing: Typically a finished black tea base reprocessed to take on lychee aroma, as with other scented teas. Some products use flavouring instead.
harvest_season: Not documented. Base tea and any scenting material come from separate harvests.
appearance_dry: Dark, fine twisted leaf, as is typical of a Chinese black tea base.
taste_profile: A soft black tea with a sweet, floral lychee aroma; low astringency is typical of the better lots, while strong added flavouring can taste like perfume.

brewing.notes: Normally brewed Western-style. Over-steeping leaves the base tea bitter under the aroma; it is also good iced.

vintage_note: Sold without vintage as a flavoured everyday tea. The aroma is the point and it fades, so buy small amounts and drink them within about a year.
description:
Lychee black tea is Chinese black tea carrying the aroma of lychee. It is a reprocessed tea rather than a strictly place-bound one, and it is usually linked with Guangdong.

The usual idea is the same as with other scented teas: finished tea absorbs aroma from fresh material, then the moisture is driven off. Detail varies by maker, and products on sale can also rely on plain flavouring.

The cup should be a soft black tea first, with sweet, faintly rosy lychee over it. A sharp sweet-shop smell usually points to flavouring. Use water just under the boil and keep steeps moderate, as long steeps bury the fruit under tannin.

There is no grading standard worth relying on, so ask how the aroma got there. Ingredient lists help: anything listing flavouring is a different product from a scented tea, even if the name on the bag is the same.
history: Little firm history is recorded for lychee black tea, and no single inventor or date is well established. It belongs to the wider Chinese practice of scenting finished tea.
